title: Jesse Cook | Rumba Flamenco Music | The Best of “Love In The Time of Covid”
description:
Jesse Cook | Rumba Flamenco Music| The Best of "Love in the Time of Covid"

I recorded these songs at home, over four months, at the height of lockdown. Music gave me a way to escape the four walls of my house. And posting these videos gave me a community of music lovers to connect with once a week during our Friday premieres. With music and friends, you can get through almost anything.

Although most of what you see here is me, alone, playing all the instruments, recording, mixing, filming and editing these videos, I was very fortunate to have friends and family who jumped in to help on a few. I am eternally grateful to: CCDOP, Nancy, Corey, both Juans, Dan, Marito, Fethi, and Matt.

The cello or violoncello is a bowed (sometimes plucked and occasionally hit) string instrument of the violin family. Played by a cellist or violoncellist, it enjoys a large solo repertoire with and without accompaniment, as well as numerous concerti. As a solo instrument, the cello uses its whole range, from bass to soprano, and in chamber music such as string quartets and the orchestra's string section, it often plays the bass part, where it may be reinforced an octave lower by the double basses. 

Among the most well-known Baroque works for the cello are Johann Sebastian Bach's six unaccompanied Suites. From the Classical era, the two concertos by Joseph Haydn in C major and D major stand out. Well-known works of the Romantic era include the Robert Schumann Concerto, the Antonín Dvořák Concerto, the first Camille Saint-Saëns Concerto, as well as the two sonatas and the Double Concerto by Johannes Brahms. A review of compositions for cello in the Romantic era must include the German composer Fanny Mendelssohn who wrote Fantasia in G Minor for cello and piano and a Capriccio in A-flat for cello.

title: Harp in a Giant Redwood Tree: 1 Hour Healing Music | Sarah Bhalla
description:
There is no feeling like being in the forest among the giant ancient redwood trees. The air shifts, like you’ve stepped into a world outside of time. Coast redwoods (Sequoia sempervirens) are the tallest beings on Earth and some of the oldest, living over 2,000 years. 

This beautiful tree endured a severe fire that hollowed out the inside. Redwood bark is incredibly fire-resistant; if enough of the tissue remains, the tree will heal and thrive.  This incredible living being draws many visitors each year, and I felt so humbled to be here, to meet both locals and travelers who love this forest. Many come here routinely to walk among the trees, to feel a connection, and to find healing. 

A few wonderful animals call the forest home, and some even sang along once the music started. Listen closely and you’ll hear owls and the playful Steller’s Jay. To sit within this towering Redwood and feel the harp’s sound vibrate through the tree, it’s hard to put that into words.  There was a deep presence in those moments, shared with the many beautiful souls I met here. This lives close to my heart, and I’m grateful to share these moments.

All of the music is improvised and includes a melody that came to me as a child. This chord structure is one I always return to, one of the first I ever improvised to, and it always feels like coming home.

So much love to you,

Sarah

title: Grateful Heart: 1 Hour of Soothing Harp Music | Sarah Bhalla
description:
How have you been? I hope you're doing well. I recorded this video a few weeks ago, and it holds a very special place in my heart. From the moment I arrived in this garden, the air was filled with the fragrance of so many beautiful flowers and a wave of deep nostalgia.

It brought back memories of my grandmother and her deep love of flowers. She tended a vibrant, abundant garden; some of my earliest and dearest memories are of walking beside her among the blooms. That feeling,  like the scent of flowers in the breeze, or the stillness of lying in the grass watching clouds drift by, surrounded me completely.

As I played, I felt as if I were playing for her, as if she were right there in the garden with me, listening. Though she has passed, her presence felt so near, carried on the breeze and in the petals around me.

title: Valley of the Waterfalls: 1 Hour of Harp Music at Yosemite National Park | Sarah Bhalla
description:
How have you been? I hope you're doing well.  I recently had the joy of recording this video in the heart of Yosemite National Park, an experience made even more special by sharing it with my mom and brother. These are moments I’ll carry with me forever.

My mom has been so supportive of my music ever since I began playing at the age of 8. It’s truly because of her unwavering support that I was able to pursue harp. She always encouraged me to practice and made incredible sacrifices for my musical journey. She would even drive up to three hours each way just to take me to lessons. I’m endlessly grateful for the belief and effort she poured into helping me grow and all of the “harp time” we spent together. So many of my childhood memories are of the two of us traveling across rural Montana for me to play at events around the state.

For their visit, we spontaneously decided to take a road trip to Yosemite National Park, which I had never been to before. What an amazing place! From the towering cliffs and cascading waterfalls to the ancient Sequoias and the peaceful river winding through the valley, it truly felt like Heaven on Earth. I’m so grateful to experience the stillness and wonder of creation there.

There’s a part of a melody I played there that has been with me since childhood, something I’ve carried in my heart, waiting for the right moment to share it. It’s a melody about overcoming, about walking through adversity with faith, and remembering that we are never alone. We are deeply loved and held by God. I’ve played it through tears many times, always feeling that same quiet reassurance, a prayer of faith and resilience.  To play it here was beyond words, and I could’ve stayed in that moment in front of these falls forever. 

Later, I learned that I had been playing in front of Yosemite Falls, the tallest known waterfall in North America, standing at an incredible 2,425 feet (739 meters). It was truly an honor to bring my harp to Yosemite, to play in the valley, and to share those incredible moments with my mom and brother.

With all my heart, thank you for your continued support, your beautiful comments, and for allowing me to share my music here.   Not too long ago, I was in a corporate role, and years passed with me playing very little. That season taught me so much, too, but I’m grateful I found my way back to the harp. Just know that it is never too late, it’s never too late to have faith, it’s never too late to dream. To be here with you is a dream come true for me, and I’m deeply grateful for you.

Soo much love to you.

title: Peaceful Harp in the Eucalyptus Forest (1 Hour) | Sarah Bhalla
description:
Learn to play the harp: https://www.sarahbhalla.com/

A day of adventure, searching for alignment and what would feel like the right place to play. Some days are more carefully planned, but it’s the moments that arrive naturally that often feel the most connected.

I wandered through a beautiful morning in the redwood forest, searching with my harp for the right spot, but somehow it wasn’t quite right, and the search continued. A beach followed, with a gentle breeze, but the ocean tide was high and the waves crashed onto the shore.

Not far from there was a lush Eucalyptus forest, full of life. The forest floor carpeted with orange, purple, and white wildflowers, with the most beautiful ray of light peeking through as if showing the way. In that moment, everything felt aligned. As the evening sun dipped lower and the fog began rolling in, I ended the session a little earlier than I would have liked to keep the harp safe. The moment is held in a loop, allowing the light, the flowers, and the feeling to stay a little longer.

I’m so grateful you’re here. Sending you so much love.

title: Turlough O'Carolan: "George Reynolds"  on Celtic Harp (Keltische Harfe)
description:
This is my contribution to the "Lockdown Turlough O'Carolan Challenge" that was initiated by Asya Sergeeva in April 2020. 

I drew the number 157, "George Reynolds", a cheerful uplifting tune that was a pleasure to arrange and to practice during the weeks of lockdown.

When thinking about where I could shoot the video for this tune, I ran across a marvelous sight right next to our local supermarket at the end of May:
a mound of soil covered with wildflowers, right next to the supermarket's parking lot!
It dawned on me that this flowery abundance had only happened thanks to the lockdown, because without doubt the mound would have otherwise been "cultivated" with other plants, bushes, lawn, or would have disappeared altogether.
So, the perfect place for a wonderful challenge that sparked joy and creativitiy during a gloomy time period.
Thank you Asya for the cool idea, thank you Turlough O'Carolan for your music that shines through the centuries, and thank you to all the harpists around the world who participated!

title: "The Days to Come" Celtic Harp Solo by Nadia Birkenstock (keltische Hafe)
description:
Find the sheet music of this original composition as PDF at https://www.keltische-harfe.de/shop/shop/pdf-sheet-music/celtic-harp-solos/the-days-to-come-pdf/

Music, audio recording and mix, video editing: Nadia Birkenstock
Filming, drone flights, audio mastering, video editing: Ralf Kleemann

The story behind the video:
In the Summer of 2020, in the middle of the Corona-Pandemic, the foundation "Klangspektrum Baden-Württemberg" launched a sponsored artist support programm for a giant video installation.
(https://klangspektrum-bw.de/)
1000 Musicians could apply with a video of a previously unreleased piece, and I chose to film "The Days to come" an instrumental piece that I had written in the previous weeks.

I had written "The days to Come" on my smaller harp, Iona, that I took into the forest, every afternoon, sitting in the shade on mossy stones.

The melody fragment that first emerged when I sat down to write this was calm and confident, and in the essence, I think, this piece is about reminding yourself where your strength comes from in challenging times. 

The filming (including the drone flights) was done in Alsace, on the Mont Sainte Odile, in the middle of August 2020 by my wonderful friend and collegue Ralf Kleemann.
A big warm thank you for his work!
Check out his YouTube channel at https://www.youtube.com/user/harfenspieler 

Hope you'll enjoy!

******************

The harp played in this video is the 35 string rosewood Celtic Harp (harpe celtique, keltische Harfe) "Manjula", made by Frank Sievert & Burkart Kleiner in Germany.

Frank Sievert sadly passed away a few years ago, but if you are looking for a simliar harp I highly recommend conatcting Reto Hofstetter who worked with him: satelier.hofstetter@gmail.com.

title: Harp Solo "Alameda" by Nadia Birkenstock (Lever harp, celtic harp, keltische Harfe)
description:
Original composition by Nadia Birkenstock
Sheet music available

“Alameda” is the Spanish word for tree-lined avenue, often in public parks, where people of all generations meet, go for a walk, relax in the shade of the trees, read, watch the people passing by, play music, dance, flirt and share life in general.
I have been inspired to this original composition by numerous trips to Spain and wanted to write something relaxed, rhythmic and groovy with a fun factor.
“Alameda” fits well into a cocktail or (student) concert repertoire and also sounds great with percussion or drums alongside.

Sheet music available here:
https://www.nadiabirkenstock.com/shop/shop/pdf-sheet-music/celtic-harp-solos/alameda-pdf/

The piece was written for a panel discussion on compising for harp of the wonderful YouTube channel “Talking Harps” where Victoria Johnson and her team connect harpists around the globe:

Welcome to my Guzheng music cover of "To Love's End" from the popular anime series Inuyasha! This beautiful and emotional piece is composed by Kaoru Wada and is a fan favorite from the show.

In this Guzheng cover, I wanted to showcase the unique sound and character of the Guzheng, a traditional Chinese instrument with a history dating back over 2,500 years. With its delicate and expressive plucking techniques, the Guzheng is the perfect instrument to capture the heartfelt melody and poignant lyrics of "To Love's End".

I hope you enjoy my rendition of this classic anime tune, and that it brings back fond memories of watching Inuyasha. Please don't forget to like, comment, and subscribe for more Guzheng covers and anime music! Thank you for listening.

title: The Best of Guzheng - Chinese Musical Instruments - Relaxing Music Part 2
description:
The Best of Guzheng - Chinese Musical Instruments - Relaxing Music Part 2
-------------------------------------------------------------------
------------------------------ Wiki -----------------------------
-------------------------------------------------------------------
The guzheng (Chinese: 古箏), also known as the Chinese zither, is a Chinese plucked string instrument with a more than 2,500-year history. It has 16 (or more) strings and movable bridges. The modern guzheng usually has 21 strings, and is 64 inches (1,600 mm) long. It has a large, resonant cavity made from wutong wood. Other components are often made from other woods for structural or decorative reasons. Guzheng players often wear fingerpicks, made from materials such as ivory, tortoiseshell, resin or hard plastic, on one or both hands.

最後，這首歌的曲譜已經免費分享到公眾號了，大家自取哦~

title: Rohan Dasgupta - Videos
description:
More info - 𝗵𝘁𝘁𝗽://𝘄𝘄𝘄.𝗿𝗼𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗮𝘀𝗴𝘂𝗽𝘁𝗮.𝗰𝗼𝗺/


Rohan has been nurturing the art of Sitar playing for nearly 30 years and remains a humble student of music.

Felicitated by 𝗬𝗮𝗱𝘂𝗯𝗵𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗮 award, 𝗦𝘂𝗿𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗶 title, 𝗣𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗶𝘁 𝗩𝗶𝘀𝗵𝗻𝘂 𝗗𝗶𝗴𝗮𝗺𝗯𝗮𝗿 award and 𝗚𝗶𝗱𝗻𝗮𝗮𝗿 𝗥𝗮𝘁𝗻𝗮 award, Rohan is a seasoned performer, composer and teacher, performed in over 16 countries across the globe including India, various European countries, Russia and South America, credited for his dynamic classical solo performances around the world and numerous international collaboration with renowned artists of various genres.

Carrying forward the legacy of one of the rarest and intricate style of Sitar ‘𝗝𝗮𝗳𝗳𝗲𝗿𝗸𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗶 𝗯𝗮𝗮𝗷’, he has presented lecture demonstrations and seminars in Santa Cecilia and Giuseppe Verdi Music conservatories in Rome and Milan respectively. He has performed in the prestigious 𝗦𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲𝗲𝘁 𝗡𝗮𝘁𝗮𝗸 𝗔𝗰𝗮𝗱𝗲𝗺𝘆 and has composed for Indian classical dance drama, classical and contemporary instrumental ensembles internationally.

Rohan :-
A rising star in the colossal realm of the Indian classical music, Rohan has enthralled audiences at home and abroad. A few notable of them are Basel university 550 years celebration in Switzerland,Indo-German music festival in Germany, EZCC music festival & Haridas Sangeet Sammelan in India, ,Parampara music festival in Suriname, South America . 
As an accomplished classical soloist and composer, Rohan has received felicitations from various esteemed organisations - some distinguished ones are the President’s award ,the Surmani title, Ravi Koppikar & Pt.Vishnudigambar award.

In the current album "Sages", Rohan discovers the deep rooted traditional values and wisdom of a sage through the meditative expressions of the morning Ragas - Ahir Bhairav and Bhairavi.This album features a special collaboration with his sister, the singing virtuoso Koyel Dasgupta Naha. The talented siblings present a light classical composition accompanied by  maestros  in traditional Indian rhythm of Tabla by Sandip Ghosh and Mridangam by Shankar Narayanswamy.The album concludes with a spriteful folk composition.


Available from October 2014.

title: '𝗨𝗣𝗔𝗝' | Rohan Dasgupta & Pt.Sanju Sahai | Raga Jhinjhoti live
description:
𝕽𝖆𝖌𝖆 𝕵𝖍𝖎𝖓𝖏𝖍𝖔𝖙𝖎 𝖎𝖓 𝕵𝖍𝖆𝖕𝖙𝖆𝖆𝖑
Sitar - Rohan Dasgupta
Tabla - Pandit Sanju Sahai

In Indian classical music extemporization of melodic/rhythmic themes based on the moment's inspiration, guided by the discipline of the Raga/Tala is called '𝗨𝗣𝗔𝗝' and such interplay between the Sitar and the Tabla often forms a spiritual trance like state.

'Upaj' is a unique performance by Sitarist Rohan Dasgupta and Tablist Sanju Sahai on 20th May 2022, Raga Jhinjhoti comes alive with a meditative and organic unfolding of the moment at the Cankarjev Dom of Ljubljana. 
The performance captures the meditative and yet joyful moments of a Raga exploration and an incredible interplay between the Sitar and the Tabla in 10 beats rhythm cycle 'Jhaptaal'. The receptive and relatively new audience of Slovenia responded with warmth and appreciation.

title: Excerpt of "Ragas, Sitar & Improvisation Explained" by Rohan Dasgupta
description:
Here is an excerpt of an interactive lecture demonstration session by Rohan Dasgupta, conducted in Slovenia as a step to educate listeners and bring them close to the art form.

Exploring Indian Classical Music: History, Structure, and Improvisation

This educational presentation offers a comprehensive insight into the rich tapestry of Indian classical music. It begins with a historical overview, tracing the evolution of this ancient musical tradition from its Vedic roots to its present-day forms—Hindustani and Carnatic.

The session then takes a pedagogical approach to understanding Raga, the foundational melodic framework in Indian music. Participants will learn how ragas function, their emotional and spiritual dimensions, and their role in shaping compositions and performances.

A special focus will be given to the Sitar, exploring its origins, construction, and the significant role it has played in the development of Indian classical music, especially within the Hindustani tradition.

The presentation also delves into the art of improvisation, demystifying how musicians creatively engage with melody and rhythm in real time. Through analysis and audio examples, learners will gain a deeper appreciation for the spontaneous yet structured nature of improvisation in Indian music.

Finally, the session encourages interactive learning and dialogue, aiming to educate and inspire open-minded listeners—whether new to Indian classical music or looking to deepen their understanding.

Artist - Rohan Dasgupta
Tanpura - Tatjana Tomazin
Venue - Cankarjev Dom, Ljubljana, Slovenia

description:
Presenting an excerpt from our Raag Yaman bandish, featuring the beautiful combination of sarangi and electric guitar. Known as the foundation raga of Hindustani classical music, Yaman's evening melody takes on a new dimension through this father-son collaboration.

Watch how the electric guitar complements the sarangi's traditional voice, creating a fusion that honors the raga's classical structure while exploring contemporary sonic possibilities. Music truly has no boundaries when it comes from the heart.

title: Raag Kirvani Complete Journey: Sarangi & Electric Guitar
description:
Experience the complete essence of Raag Kirvani in this 12-minute musical journey that showcases the raga's profound depth and contemplative beauty.

This comprehensive presentation unfolds Kirvani's intricate character through both traditional sarangi and electric guitar, creating a unique sonic landscape while maintaining the raga's classical integrity. From the meditative opening alaap that explores Kirvani's fundamental nature, to the structured bandish that reveals its emotional core, every moment captures the raga's introspective and deeply moving qualities.

Kirvani, renowned for its gentle curves and contemplative spirit, offers the ideal framework for this innovative instrumental combination. The sarangi's traditional voice interweaves seamlessly with the electric guitar's contemporary tones, proving that Hindustani classical music can embrace new instruments while preserving its ancient wisdom.

This complete rendition demonstrates how ragas transcend instrumental boundaries, speaking directly to the soul regardless of the medium. The result is a mesmerizing exploration of one of Indian classical music's most beautiful and emotionally rich ragas.

🎵 Complete Raga Development: Alaap to Bandish
🎻 Traditional Sarangi Mastery
🎸 Electric Guitar Innovation
⏱️ 12 Minutes of Pure Classical Expression

title: Saadoun Al-Bayati in concert UNC-Chapel Hill  سعدون البياتي
description:
Saadoun Al-Bayati, born in Baghdad, Iraq, is the son of an ardhahalchi or paralegal fluent in Arabic, Turkish and Kurdish and a Sufi woman of the Na'imiyya order. As a child, while attending Sufi rituals and ceremonies with his mother and maternal uncle, Shaykh Jasim Abd al-Sittar, Saadoun was exposed to the meditative states produced through sustained percussion and vocalizing.

His voice training took place through Qur'anic recitation in which fine precision in achieving correct tones and articulation of words in required. As a young man, Saadoun often substituted for the muezzin at his neighborhood mosque in the Al-Fadhl section of Old Baghdad, calling Muslims to prayer. Having internalized the spiritual essence of a Middle Eastern/Islamic aesthetic, Saadoun has performed the music of Iraq and other parts of the Arab Middle East since childhood.

In the United States Saadoun pursued studies in acting and graduated from the Goodman Theatre at the Art Institute of Chicago. His many accomplishments as an actor included playing Dr. Aziz to Lillian Gish's Mrs. Moore in "A Passage to India" and working with such theatrical talents as Morris Carnovsky in "Mother Courage" and "King Lear "and Sam Wanamaker in "MacBeth."

But throughout his life and studies, music has been a focal point for his intense musical energies. Saadoun thus decided to learn the oud or unfretted version of the lute, initially to better understand the musical structures of Middle Eastern music -- specifically the maqamat or modal structures, with their distinct ascending and descending scales -- and eventually to provide a reliable support for his singing voice (not easy, when one has perfect pitch). Saadoun was fortunate to be able to learn from close personal friends such as the pre-eminent Nubian musician Hamza El-Din, the Lebanese musician George Khayyat, and the Syrian oud-player Hussny El-Zaim.

He has performed at concerts and night clubs in many parts of the United States. Saadoun's unique musical expression emanates from the depth of his soul and transcends all geographical boundaries. A voice that stirs profound emotions and a technique that is at once powerful and sensuous represent the highest level of artistic expression.

title: بداهه نوازی در دستگاه چهارگاه - Persian Traditional Classical Music - Improvisation in Chahargah
description:
This is an improvisation piece based on Persian or Iranian traditional classical music. The instrument is called "TAR" consisted of 6 strings. 

Persian or Iranian traditional classical music is consisted of 12 modal scales and tunes named 7 main "dastgāh" and 5 derivative "āvāz". This whole body is called radif, of which there are several versions, each in accordance to the teachings of a particular master (ostād). Source: Wikipedia. Each dastgāh consists of seven basic notes, plus several variable notes used for ornamentation and modulation. Each dastgāh is a certain modal variety subject to a course of development (sayr) that is determined by the pre-established order of sequences, and revolves around 365 central nuclear melodies known as gushehs (each of these melodies being a gusheh), which musicians come to know through experience and absorption. This process of centonization is personal, and it is a tradition of great subtlety and depth. The full collection of gushehs in all dastgāhs is referred to as the radif. 

Radifs were officially registered on the UNESCO List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

The tradition dates back to Barbad. Barbad was the most famous and skilled court musician of the Sassanid Empire of Persia. Barbad is remembered in many documents and has been named as a remarkably high skilled musician of his time. He has been credited to have given an organization of musical system consisting of seven "Royal modes" named Xosrovani (Persian: سرود خسروانى‎), thirty derivative modes named lahn, and 360 melodies named dastan. These numbers are in accordance with Sassanid's calendar of number of days in a week, month, and year. Source: Wikipedia.

In this music similar to ancient Greek music quarter tone and tetra cords are used. In traditional music theory, a tetrachord always spanned the interval of a perfect fourth, a 4:3 frequency proportion (approx. 498 cents). Persian music divides the interval of a fourth differently than the Greek. For example, one of the iconic scholar of Islamic, era Al-Farabi describes four genres of the division of the fourth:
The first genre, corresponding to the Greek diatonic, is composed of a tone, a tone and a semitone, as G–A–B–C.
The second genre is composed of a tone, three quarter tones and three quarter tones, as G–A–B half flat –C.
The third genre has a tone and a quarter, three quarter tones and a semitone, as G–A half sharp –B–C.
The fourth genre, corresponding to the Greek chromatic, has a tone and a half, a semitone and a semitone, as G–A♯–B–C.

Later, he presents possible positions of the frets on the lute, producing ten intervals dividing the interval of a fourth between the strings:
Ratio: 1/1 256/243 18/17 162/149 54/49 9/8 32/27 81/68 27/22 81/64 4/3
Note name: C C♯ C♯ Cthree quarter sharp Cthree quarter sharp D E♭ E♭ Ehalf flat E F
Cents: 0 90 99 145 168 204 294 303 355 408 498

If one considers that the interval of a fourth between the strings of the lute (Oud) corresponds to a tetrachord, and that there are two tetrachords and a major tone in an octave, this would create a 25-tone scale. A more inclusive description (where Ottoman, Persian and Arabic overlap), of the scale divisions is that of 24 quarter tones (see also Arabian maqam). It should be mentioned that Al-Farabi's, among other Islamic treatises, also contained additional division schemes as well as providing a gloss of the Greek system as Aristoxenian doctrines were often included.

title: تقسيم حجاز كار - منير بشير Taqsim Hijaz Kar - Munir Bashir
description:
The late Iraqi 'ud player Munir Bashir, whose style is influenced by the artistry of his Turkish trained teacher Sharif Muhyi al-Din Haydar, presents a highly lyrical style which unlike the traditional mainstream of Arab 'ud playing appears seamless, thus avoiding clear cut qaflat and phrase delineations. Many of hhis typically long performances stay in the same maqam and maintain a subdued, meditative mood quite consistently. Listeners sometimes speak of non-Arab influences on his style, including North Indian ragas and jazz. Having performed in various major cities in Asia, Europe and North America, Bashir has created improvisatory works that are intended to evoke specific impressions, for example those of ancient Babylon. Deriving significantly from the Iraqi modal tradition, Bashir's style is also highly ambient. Employing subtle but effective dynamic inflections and a gradual build up in the intensity of picking, his playing is known to demand quiet concentration on the part of the listeners.*

* Racy, Ali Jihad. "The Many Faces of Improvisation: The Arab Taqasim as a Musical Symbol." Ethnomusicology 44 (2000): 313.

Visiting maestro, Ustad Raza Ali Khan is the custodian of Kasur-Patiala gharana’s illustrious legacy. The son of Ustad Munawwar Ali Khan & grandson to the indomitable Ustad Bade Ghulam Ali Khan sahib, Ustad Raza Ali Khan inherits a strong, tradition of khayal and thumri from his forefathers.
Ustad Raza Ali Khan received training from Ustad Bade Ghulam Ali Khan until his death and thereafter from his father Ustad Munawar Ali Khan. Ustad Raza Ali Khan manifests all the defining characteristics of his gharana’s gayeki in his adayegi, use of khatka & gamak, tez sargam and intricate taans in the performances.

Umeed Ali Khan (1910 - 1979)

"Like his father (Ustad Piyare Khan), Umeed Ali Khan was also gifted with sweet, rich, lively and forceful voice, which he dexterously used in the promotion of Gowaliar style of classical singing. Years of hard training under the supervision of his father made Umeed Ali Khan's style highly sophisticated and refined.

"From late 1930s to the middle of 1970s, Ustad Umeed Ali Khan ranked high in the hierarchy of classical vocalists of the sub-continent. He was known for his passion and ability for promoting and popularising the Gwalior gharana style of kheyal singing.

Until his death, Ustad Umeed Ali Khan remained a faithful exponent of the Gowaliar gharana of kheyal singing, a trait which he also passed on to his disciples, including the classical duo of Fateh Ali Khan-Hameed Ali Khan of Hyderabad, Sindh. Another follower of the Gowaliar clan of musicians is composer Master Manzoor Husain.

During his prime, the late Ustad Umeed Ali Khan excelled a number of his contemporaries in the rendition of taranas, thumris and dadras. His mature and deep musical insight were augmented by his refined melodic thinking and acute sensitivity. Handsome vocalist late Ustad Umeed Ali Khan developed a good taste for clothing and living in a style."

description: Raga Hamsadhwani is a beautiful Raga which draws inspiration from Carnatic Music. A raga under the thaat Bilawal, it is similar to the western Ionian mode (a subset of Ionian, in fact). Hamsadhwani literally translates to Sound of the swans. The presiding deity of the Raga is Lord Vishnu, source of Sattva, or positive, sublime energy. Hence, its name Sattva is an apt representation of its peaceful and sublime nature. The raga is traditionally performed in the evenings, and that's when the Raga has its maximum effect. He is an award-winning American western and Hindustani classically trained cellist, composer & producer. Based between New York and Mumbai, specializing in cinematic music with an emphasis on orchestral and Indian influences. Co-founder of Rose Productions.

He is a disciple of the renowned violinist Padmabhushan Dr. N. Rajam in the rare Gayaki Ang style and is one of the few cellists in the world performing Indian music on the cello.

Jake Charkey Bio:
He studied cello in the Western Classical tradition under Paul Cohen, Leopold Teraspulsky, and finally with Norman Fischer at the Shepherd School of music at Rice University in Houston, TX. Seeking to broaden his musical skills and vocabulary after conservatory training, he took an interest in Hindustani music. His studies began in Toronto with the sarangi player, Aruna Narayan, who urged him to adapt Hindustani music to cello rather than learn an Indian instrument.  He continued in Los Angeles where he took up intensive training with Jagan Ramamoorthy, a senior disciple of the violin virtuoso Padmabushan Dr. N. Rajam.  He completed his M.F.A. at CalArts in Hindustani music under the guidance of Aashish Khan and Swapan Chaudhuri and with additional instruction on cello and contemporary techniques from Erika Duke-Kirkpatrick.  While at Cal-Arts he also incorporated other modalities of improvisation into his playing with Vinny Golia, Wadada Leo Smith, and Charlie Haden.

After grad school, Jake moved to Montreal, where continued to perform Hindustani music, both as a soloist and accompanist for Kathak dance, and was an occasional collaborator with tUnEyArds.  In 2010 he traveled to India with an arts fellowship from the Shastri Indo-Canadian Institute to support formal study under Padmabushan Dr. N. Rajam with whom he continued to learn for the 6 years he stayed there.

He recorded for dozens of Indian films and performed with many of the most celebrated musicians in Bollywood including artists like Zakir Hussain, Hariharan, Yesudas, Arijit Singh, and Master Saleem, among many others. He is an award-winning American western and Hindustani classically trained cellist, composer & producer. Based between New York and Mumbai, specializing in cinematic music with an emphasis on orchestral and Indian influences. Co-founder of Rose Productions.

Jake Charkey Bio:
He studied cello in the Western Classical tradition under Paul Cohen, Leopold Teraspulsky, and finally with Norman Fischer at the Shepherd School of music at Rice University in Houston, TX. Seeking to broaden his musical skills and vocabulary after conservatory training, he took an interest in Hindustani music. His studies began in Toronto with the sarangi player, Aruna Narayan, who urged him to adapt Hindustani music to cello rather than learn an Indian instrument.  He continued in Los Angeles where he took up intensive training with Jagan Ramamoorthy, a senior disciple of the violin virtuoso Padmabushan Dr. N. Rajam.  He completed his M.F.A. at CalArts in Hindustani music under the guidance of Aashish Khan and Swapan Chaudhuri and with additional instruction on cello and contemporary techniques from Erika Duke-Kirkpatrick.  While at Cal-Arts he also incorporated other modalities of improvisation into his playing with Vinny Golia, Wadada Leo Smith, and Charlie Haden.

After grad school, Jake moved to Montreal, where continued to perform Hindustani music, both as a soloist and accompanist for Kathak dance, and was an occasional collaborator with tUnEyArds.  In 2010 he traveled to India with an arts fellowship from the Shastri Indo-Canadian Institute to support formal study under Padmabushan Dr. N. "Shahid Parvez Khan is widely recognized as one of the greatest sitar players of the world.  The recipient of numerous prestigious awards, including the  Government of India's Padma Shri and the Sangeet Natak Academy Award,  Shahid Parvez Khan regularly tours across India, Europe, North America,  Asia and Australia, enthralling audiences everywhere.  

 Shahid Parvez’s music is both novel and evolving.  His unique tone and astute artistic sense have become his hallmark as a respected performer and composer.  The power of his music emanates from the highly charged sound he conjures on stage.  He emphasizes the unique capabilities of this sitar itself while  drawing upon numerous musical influences easily recognizable to a  knowing ear.  He has achieved success in not only preserving tradition, but  also pushing its boundaries to even greater heights of aesthetic beauty. 

 Shahid Parvez Khan represents the seventh generation of the sitar’s first family, the Etawah Gharana.  A very young Shahid Parvez was initiated into the rich  traditions of the Gharana by his father and guru, Ustad Aziz Khan - the  famous musician and son of legendary sitar and surbahar virtuoso Ustad  Waheed Khan.  His family has produced the most revered and influential figures  in Hindustani Classical Music including Ustad Sahabdad Khan, Ustad Imdad  Khan, Ustad Enayet Khan, and Ustad Vilayat Khan."

title: Sattva | Raga Hamsadhwani | Exploration and improvisation on Sitar
description: Raga Hamsadhwani is a beautiful Raga which draws inspiration from Carnatic Music. A raga under the thaat Bilawal, it is similar to the western Ionian mode (a subset of Ionian, in fact). Hamsadhwani literally translates to Sound of the swans. The presiding deity of the Raga is Lord Vishnu, source of Sattva, or positive, sublime energy. Hence, its name Sattva is an apt representation of its peaceful and sublime nature. The raga is traditionally performed in the evenings, and that's when the Raga has its maximum effect. The Raga's Rasa (emotional theme and mental state of the Raga) is auspicious.

description:
Rāga Rāmkali is one of the early morning Rāgas (Time: 3 - 6 am). It belongs to Thāt Bhairav. I tried improvising using my limited understanding of the notes which are present in the Rāga. 

The Rāga is very meditative, devotional and is related to the classical Indian concept of Viraha/an emotion arising out of separation of a loved one.
